page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.A4.Ax.Flex.2-32 is an Arm-based instance configuration within the Standard family. Powered by an Ampere AmpereOne-M processor running the arm64 architecture, this instance allocates 4 dedicated physical cores with 1 thread per core, resulting in 4 vCPUs. The lack of simultaneous multithreading ensures that each core executes instructions independently without shared hardware resource contention.

System memory totals 32.0 GB, providing an elevated memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated local disk storage, necessitating the use of attached cloud block storage for persistent filesystems, and it contains no discrete GPU accelerators. Network provisioning includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Because it provides 8 GB of RAM per vCPU, this instance offers high memory density relative to core count without requiring oversized compute allocations. It is suitable for memory-intensive workloads such as in-memory caches, intermediate databases, and Arm-native application backends that prioritize memory capacity over large parallel compute footprints.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.A4.Ax.Flex.2-32 is an arm64-based compute instance built on the Ampere AmpereOne-M processor platform. The server provides 4 physical cores and 4 vCPUs with dedicated, single-threaded execution, coupled with 32.0 GB of system memory to achieve a memory density of 8.0 GB per core. The configuration includes no onboard local storage, depending entirely on remote block storage solutions for disk operations, and contains zero GPU acceleration hardware. A single complimentary public IPv4 address is provisioned by default. With its high memory-to-vCPU allocation, VM.Standard.A4.Ax.Flex.2-32 provides an efficient operational profile for memory-sensitive environments that do not require massive parallel compute threads. It is well matched for in-memory caching systems, distributed data processing nodes, intermediate database deployments, and Arm-native web application stacks.
